extracted.intended_audience: individuals applying for registration to practice before the USPTO (prospective patent agents/attorneys) and USPTO OED decisionmakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used by the USPTO (OED and Director) to determine whether an applicant 'possesses good moral character and reputation' for registration to practice before the Office, and the related procedural rules for petitioning an OED decision. Covers what evidence counts, how credibility is assessed, and procedural deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement to show good moral character and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recognition as a representative the applicant 'must show that they are of good moral character and reputation' (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D); implemented in 37 C.F.R. § 11.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director must be satisfied that the applicant possesses good moral character and reputation before registration will be granted; this statutory/regulatory standard is the threshold for the entire evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bears the burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner/applicant bears the burden of demonstrating that he or she possesses the good moral character to practice before the USPTO (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED informs applicants they must produce evidence to meet this burden; absence of persuasive evidence supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'good moral character' (Konigsberg standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Good moral character' denotes 'an absence of proven conduct or acts which have been historically considered as manifestations of "moral turpitude."' (citing Konigsberg v. State Bar of California).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations focus on whether proven conduct (e.g., dishonesty, fraud, misrepresentation) reflects moral turpitude; the historical concept guides assessment of particular acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory questions and evidence per 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED considers evidence presented by the applicant in answer to questions authorized by 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g) when determining present possession of good moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should answer the authorized questions fully and support answers with credible, corroborating evidence; responses are part of the record used to judge character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and procedural requirements for petitioning an OED decision
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to the USPTO Director under 37 C.F.R. § 11.2(d) must be accompanied by the appropriate fee and filed within sixty days of the mailing date of the OED Director's final decision; petitions not filed within sixty days will be dismissed as untimely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 60-day filing deadline and fee requirement — failure to comply results in dismissal of appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and reliability of documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents submitted by the applicant must be credible; OED will assess technical provenance (e.g., whether screenshots show Word/Adobe file properties rather than native OACS creation timestamps) and whether documents could have been created/modified off-site and later uploaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents that can be shown to originate outside Office systems or that are altered without disclosure are not reliable; applicants should provide corroborating documentation (e.g., native-system artifacts or other saved-work evidence) to establish presence or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration requirement for assertions about being on-premises or working
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenshots or file properties alone will be insufficient absent corroboration; lack of other contemporaneous Office-created items (e.g., saved searches) weakens the applicant's claim of being on campus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present multiple, independent forms of contemporaneous evidence showing presence/work in USPTO systems to strengthen claims; single altered files are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of misrepresentation and successive misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional misrepresentation of time and attendance (claiming pay for hours not worked) weighs strongly against finding good moral character; submitting altered documents or otherwise perpetuating the misrepresentation during the investigation compounds the adverse weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An initial misrepresentation plus a later misrepresentation during the investigative process substantially undermines credibility and is likely to control the outcome unless overwhelmingly rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of siso (swipe in/swipe out) records as timekeeping evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Siso records are considered reliable evidence of physical presence; challenges to their accuracy require affirmative, specific evidence (e.g., testimony that the applicant was allowed in without swiping, malfunction records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General assertions that the system sometimes failed or that a policy changed do not, by themselves, render siso records unreliable; to rebut siso records an applicant must produce direct evidence (security testimony, proof of system malfunction, or Office policy documentation showing exception that applies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor certification of timesheets is ministerial and not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supervisor certifies an employee's timesheet, the supervisor is performing a ministerial task and relies on the employee's statement; a supervisor's certification does not corroborate the employee's actual presence if the supervisor lacks recollection or independent records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot rely solely on a supervisor's signature to establish presence; the supervisor's lack of recollection or absence of meeting records negates the certification's probative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary employee restrictions and off-site work policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Probationary employees are not authorized to work outside USPTO facilities; doing work off-site (and later transferring files into Office systems) would violate policy and is not an acceptable explanation for absence from premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if work product exists, unauthorized off-site work during probation is misconduct; applicants should not rely on off-site creation excuses for unexplained absences during probation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity/performance does not excuse dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of satisfactory or superior job performance (e.g., meeting/exceeding production goals, awards) is not a defense to falsifying time and attendance or other dishonest conduct and is not persuasive to establish moral character in the face of such misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should not expect productivity metrics to neutralize proven dishonest acts; documentation of performance is relevant but not determinative when honesty is at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on relying on Office policy changes or anecdotal acquittals
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in swipe-policy (e.g., later removal of swipe-out requirement) or anecdotal references to acquittals in unrelated criminal cases do not, by themselves, establish that siso records are unreliable or that conduct was permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must link policy changes or cases directly and specifically to their circumstances with supporting evidence; mere references are insufficient to rebut OED's factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of witness affidavits and subsequent rehabilitation evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits and testimony attesting to present good character or later accomplishments (law school, community involvement) are considered but can be outweighed by proven dishonest conduct, particularly if the witnesses lack first-hand knowledge of the disputed events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehabilitative evidence and character affidavits should ideally address the specific misconduct, provide first-hand knowledge where possible, and convincingly explain rehabilitation; otherwise, recent or unaddressed misrepresentations will predominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert/system testimony may rebut applicant's document explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may rely on testimony from system creators/experts (e.g., OACS creator) explaining how documents may be created externally and imported, undermining applicant explanations based on file properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant's documentary evidence can be explained by ordinary system behavior (imports, changed filenames), expert testimony about system operation will diminish the probative value of those documents; applicants should anticipate and rebut such technical explanations with stronger evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reapplication standard after denial
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant wishes to reapply for registration after denial, they 'must present evidence demonstrating good moral character and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later application needs clear, convincing, and demonstrative evidence of present good moral character that overcomes the prior adverse findings.
